sections.h2: Who keeps property records in Miami-Dade County
sections.html:
The Clerk of the Circuit Court and Comptroller serves as county recorder. Under Chapter 28 of the Florida Statutes, the clerk records every instrument the law allows to be recorded here.

The Official Records hold deeds, mortgages, liens, certain affidavits, subdivision plats, judgments, declarations of domicile, satisfactions and releases, powers of attorney and financial statements. Fees and transfer taxes are figured and collected when a document is recorded.

The clerk's online Official Records search covers every instrument above. Search by name, or by book and page when you already have a reference.

  • Name searches work for grantors, grantees and lienholders. Try every spelling of a name, and add the folio number when you have it.
  • Credit bureaus pick up liens and judgments recorded here. If a bureau reports one you do not recognize, ask for its book and page and request a copy from the Records Library.
  • The clerk runs a free fraud alert that notifies an owner within a day whenever a deed or mortgage is filed against the owner's name.

Most documents cost $10 for the first page and $8.50 for each additional page. A lis pendens costs $5 for the first page and $4 for each additional page.

sections.h2: Why the county fee differs from the state statute
sections.html:
Florida's clerk fee statute prints $5.00 for the first page and $4.00 for each added page of an instrument up to 14 by 8.5 inches, plus $1.00 for each name beyond four. It adds a $1.00 modernization charge on the first page and $0.50 on later pages, and an extra $4 per page for technology.

Plats run $30.00 for the first page and $15.00 for each added page, and processing a tax deed application costs $60.00. The Miami-Dade clerk publishes all-in figures, which is why the county's first-page fee reads $10. Give your title agent the clerk's current schedule instead of adding the statute lines yourself.

sections.h2: Documentary stamp tax on a deed
sections.html:
Deed stamps are 60 cents per $100 of consideration, rounded up to the next hundred. Miami-Dade is the only county that uses 60 cents in place of the standard 70.

A separate surtax of 45 cents per $100 applies to transfers of real property other than a single-family residence. Mortgages pay 35 cents per $100 of the note, plus intangible tax of $2 per $1,000.

Every party to a deed is liable for the tax under state rules, whoever agrees to pay. Your contract with the buyer sets the practical split.

sections.h2: What goes on a mortgage, satisfaction or lien filing
sections.html:
Mortgage filings must be original, signed and notarized. Attach a copy of the note, or write the note amount across the face of the mortgage. The filing needs addresses for lender and borrower and a Prepared By line.

  • A satisfaction or release needs the book and page of the mortgage, the holder's signature and a notarized acknowledgement.
  • An assignment of mortgage needs the book and page, the assignor's signature and a notary.
  • A construction lien needs the lienor's signature, a notary and a legal description or property address.

A seller paying off a loan should confirm the satisfaction is recorded, then search Official Records to see it indexed.

A quit claim deed, a deed given in place of foreclosure and a contract for deed are all on the revenue department's list of taxable documents. An executor's deed under a probated will is treated as not taxable.

A foreclosure certificate of title is taxed on the highest and best bid. A lis pendens, the notice that a foreclosure suit is pending, records at $5 for the first page. Searching for one early can warn a buyer that a lender has gone to court. In any distressed transfer, pull the title record before signing so every lien is in view.

sections.h2: What a Miami-Dade deed must include
sections.html:
The clerk's deed checklist is specific, and a missing item gets a document returned.

  • An original document with the seller's signature.
  • Addresses for grantors and grantees.
  • Two witnesses not related to the transaction, with each name and post office address printed beneath the signature.
  • A full notary acknowledgement.
  • A Prepared By statement with name and address.
  • Documentary stamps, plus the property transfer form.
  • A folio number, which is encouraged but not required, and a self-addressed stamped envelope.

Section 689.01 of the Florida Statutes separately requires two subscribing witnesses on a conveyance.

sections.h2: Filing in person, by mail or electronically
sections.html:
There are four routes. Bring the original and fees to the Osvaldo N. Soto Miami-Dade Justice Center, mail it to the Office of County Recorder at 20 NW 1st Avenue, Suite 5.246, Miami, FL 33128, use an approved eRecording vendor, or use the clerk's eRecording Web Service for Notices of Commencement and Declarations of Domicile.

Electronic filings take roughly 1 to 3 business days, excluding weekends and holidays, before they appear online. Same-day recording is not promised, so bring time-sensitive documents in person.

Cash is accepted only in person. Credit cards are in person only, with a $5,000 daily limit.

sections.h2: Removing a Social Security number from a public record
sections.html:
You can ask. The clerk accepts requests to redact Social Security, bank account and credit card numbers from documents that are available online, using its online redaction form with the file number or book and page.

People covered by Chapter 119 exemptions can file a confidentiality request, in person or online. Party names stay in the index unless the name includes a street address, as in some trusts or LLCs.

Miami-Dade has 1,125,274 housing units, and the filing load is heavy, so a clean document matters. Compare the folio and legal description with your prior deed, line up witnesses and a notary before the signing, and confirm the fees with the clerk on the day. After closing, search Official Records under your name to see that the deed and any satisfaction appear.

If you need a copy of a recorded item for a lender or title agent, ask the clerk for a certified copy rather than printing a search screen. Keep the recorded copy of your deed, the settlement statement and any payoff letters together in one folder for later tax and title questions.

faqs.q: Where do I file a deed in Miami-Dade?
faqs.a: At the County Recorder's Office, 20 NW 1st Avenue, Suite 5.246, Miami, or through an approved eRecording vendor. The clerk accepts mail and in-person filings as well.

faqs.q: What does the clerk charge to file a Miami-Dade deed?
faqs.a: The clerk lists $10 for the first page and $8.50 for each additional page, before documentary stamps. The state statute prints a lower base and allows other charges on top, so quote the clerk's list.

faqs.q: Does Miami-Dade charge a deed surtax on a house?
faqs.a: The 45 cents per $100 surtax applies to real property other than a single-family residence, so a deed for only a single-family home does not carry it.

faqs.q: Do I have to record a deed after a sale?
faqs.a: Recording gives the public notice of the transfer. Ask the title agent to record promptly, and search Official Records afterward to confirm the deed appears.

faqs.q: How long does eRecording take in Miami-Dade?
faqs.a: Roughly 1 to 3 business days before the document is viewable online.
